blocks.text: This is said against Buxtorf, who holds that the Talmudists' חוממון was formed from a Greek word (in the Lexicon Chald. p. 782). Certainly the meaning sand is in no common use in any of the other cognate dialects.

But this whole discussion rests on the opinion that חומט means sand; and no foundation could be weaker than that, see above note 1. Among the Chaldeans the verb חמט denotes he bent, curved, bent himself. Hence perhaps the caterpillar is called خُمَّاطٌ [khummāṭ] by the Arabs (see Golius, Lexic. p. 652), unless it was rather named from the fact that it gnaws plants; for خَمَطَ [khamaṭa] means he stripped the bark from a tree. But from bending the snail could also have got its name, which some of the learned favoured at Levit. XI, 30. (see Bochart at the beginning of this Chapter). You are thus taught by a new example how vain a thing it is to derive the meanings of names that designate animals from etymologies alone.
